tasks.instruction: Write a discussion response. An effective response contains at least 100 words.

professor.name: Doctor Achebe
professor.text: This week, we'll look at how well students transition to university. Many recent high school graduates have taken a gap year—a yearlong break after graduation—before studying at a university. During a gap year, students may get jobs, travel, or simply relax and think about their future. Some students say their gap year was beneficial, while others regret having taken one. In your opinion, does taking a gap year create more advantages or disadvantages for students? Why?

posts.name: Andrew
posts.text: The gap year would be a good opportunity for students to reflect on their education goals and confirm their plans for university. At least it would give someone time to investigate different fields and get a better sense of what it means to be in business, to work in an office, or to work with their hands, etc.

posts.name: Claire
posts.text: Because university can be expensive, students should not take a gap year. Tuition, the cost of books, and living expenses rise every year. The money a student might save during a gap year might not be enough to cover the rise in prices when they enter university a year later.

tasks.sample: I think it is a good idea for students to take a gap year. I agree with Andrew that taking a gap year allows high school graduates to reflect on their education goals and university plans. By spending a year working part-time and figuring out their interests, capabilities, and goals, high school graduates can have a better idea of what they are going to study in university and make the right decisions. By contrast, if students attend university right after graduating from high school, it is highly likely that many students do not have a clear clue about their future paths. This is because high school students do not have a lot of opportunities to know about society and think about their academic and professional plans. As a result, high school graduates might end up picking the wrong majors. For example, some might study finance or computer science merely because majors like these are popular rather than because they are a good fit. In fact, they might not like their major at all. It might turn out to be a waste of time and university tuition. The cost of books and living expenses do rise every year, as Claire says, but rushing to attend university and choosing the wrong major would cause a more terrible waste. (216 words)
